guide_enrichment.narrative:
For us, the disagreement starts with LSU’s defense. Our efficiency numbers rate LSU among the strongest units nationally against both the run and pass, while Mississippi State has been closer to the middle of the pack in both areas. The early results support that view: LSU allowed 142 yards per game through two games, recorded 12 sacks and held opponents to 4-of-27 on third down. That short sample is not proof, but it illustrates how LSU can control field position and create separation.

The uncertainty comes on the other side. LSU has played at high volume and converted 19 of 33 third downs, but its scoring-opportunity creation has not been especially strong in our numbers. Mississippi State’s ability to prevent those opportunities grades poorly, which helps explain why our model is more favorable toward LSU than the market. Still, LSU committed five turnovers through two games, including four interceptions. That volatility matters when laying a substantial number, and the available price does not give us enough value to move beyond a pass.
guide_enrichment.matchup_to_watch:
We are watching Mississippi State’s offense against LSU’s front. LSU allowed only 18 rushing yards per game through its first two contests, while Princewill Umanmielen produced five sacks and 6.5 tackles for loss. Our matchup numbers also identify clear advantages for LSU against both the run and pass.

If Mississippi State cannot stay ahead of the chains, LSU’s pressure can turn manageable possessions into short drives. That is the clearest football path to the margin our model sees, even though the current price leaves too little room for us to bet it.

recent_game.fact: LSU improved to 2-0 with a 45-14 win over Louisiana Tech on September 12, scoring 28 unanswered points in the second half.
LSU held Louisiana Tech to 139 total yards, eight first downs and minus-4 rushing yards.
Sam Leavitt passed for 344 yards and one touchdown and rushed for three touchdowns against Louisiana Tech.
Linebacker TJ Dottery had a team-high nine tackles against Louisiana Tech, while Princewill Umanmielen recorded three sacks.

quarterback.fact: Starting quarterback Sam Leavitt, an Arizona State transfer, completed 41 of 66 passes for 574 yards, two touchdowns and four interceptions through LSU's first two games.
Leavitt rushed for 135 yards and five touchdowns through two games and ranked second in the SEC with 354.5 total offense yards per game.
Leavitt's 344 passing yards and three rushing touchdowns against Louisiana Tech were both career highs.
Leavitt arrived at LSU with 20 previous starts at Arizona State, where the Sun Devils went 16-4 in his starts.

offensive_personnel.fact: Running back Dilin Jones led LSU through two games with 179 rushing yards and two touchdowns.
Tight end Trey'Dez Green had 10 receptions for 162 yards and one touchdown through two games; eight of his receptions produced either a first down or touchdown.

LSU's offensive starters in each of the first two games were Jordan Seaton at left tackle, Bo Bordelon at left guard, Braelin Moore at center, Aliou Bah at right guard, Weston Davis at right tackle, Trey'Dez Green at tight end, Eugene Wilson III and Winston Watkins Jr. at receiver, Dilin Jones at running back and Sam Leavitt at quarterback; Malik Elzy and Jackson Harris split the remaining receiver starts.
Left tackle Jordan Seaton transferred from Colorado after starting 22 games and playing 1,421 offensive snaps, all at left tackle.
Center Braelin Moore returned after starting all 13 games for LSU in 2025, playing 623 offensive snaps and allowing one sack.
Right guard Aliou Bah transferred from Maryland with 24 consecutive starts and more than 1,500 collegiate snaps at right guard.
Fourteen players made their first LSU starts during the opening two games, including 13 transfers and true freshman defensive tackle Deuce Geralds.

defensive_personnel.fact: EDGE Princewill Umanmielen led the nation through two games with five sacks and 6.5 tackles for loss.

LSU used the same defensive starting lineup in each of its first two games: Princewill Umanmielen and Jordan Ross at EDGE; Stephiylan Green and Deuce Geralds at defensive tackle; Whit Weeks and TJ Dottery at linebacker; PJ Woodland and DJ Pickett at cornerback; Tamarcus Cooley at free safety; Ty Benefield at rover; and Dashawn Spears at star.
TJ Dottery led LSU with 14 tackles through two games, followed by Whit Weeks with 13.
LSU returned three starters from its 2025 secondary: cornerbacks PJ Woodland and DJ Pickett and safety Tamarcus Cooley. That 2025 defense recorded 17 interceptions and allowed 14 touchdown passes.
Safety Ty Benefield transferred from Boise State with 33 career starts, 235 tackles, 18 tackles for loss, 16 pass breakups and five interceptions.

coaching_changes.fact: Lane Kiffin is in his first season as LSU's head coach after being hired on November 30, 2025.
Charlie Weis Jr. is LSU's first-year offensive coordinator and works from the press box.
Blake Baker remains LSU's defensive coordinator and is in his fourth year on the LSU staff.
Eric Wolford is LSU's first-year offensive line coach, while James Cregg serves as run game specialist for the offensive line.
Chris Kiffin joined the staff as co-defensive coordinator and linebackers coach, and Joe Houston joined as special teams coordinator.

LSU rushed for 456 yards and eight touchdowns through two games, averaging 4.5 yards per carry.
LSU outscored its first two opponents 27-3 in the first quarter.
